questions.prompt: Why does `Widget w();` inside a function fail when you subsequently call `w.run()`?
options: `Widget w();` declares a function named `w` taking no arguments and returning `Widget`, not a variable.
Parentheses can only initialize fundamental types, not classes.
questions.explanation: Under C++'s ambiguity resolution (the most vexing parse, [stmt.ambig]), any statement that can be parsed as a declaration is parsed as a declaration—so `Widget w();` declares a function `w()`. Using `Widget w{};` or `Widget w;` constructs an object.

questions.prompt: Given `std::vector<int> a(4, 9);` and `std::vector<int> b{4, 9};`, what are the sizes of `a` and `b`?
questions.explanation: Parentheses `a(4, 9)` invoke `std::vector(size_type count, const int& value)`, creating 4 copies of 9. Braces `b{4, 9}` trigger `[over.match.list]`, strongly preferring `std::vector(std::initializer_list<int>)` and creating 2 elements.

questions.prompt: Which initialization is well-formed in C++20/23 given `struct Box { explicit Box(int) {} };`?
questions.explanation: `Box b{5};` is direct-list-initialization, which allows `explicit` constructors. All three other forms (`= 5`, `= {5}`, and passing `{5}` to a parameter) are copy-initialization or copy-list-initialization, which reject `explicit` constructors under [over.match.list].

questions.prompt: What is the value of `a.x` and `b.x` after running this C++23 function?
options: Both `a.x` and `b.x` are guaranteed to be 0.
questions.explanation: Value-initialization (`{}`) zero-initializes `A` first because `A` has no user-provided or deleted default constructor, setting `a.x` to 0. Because `B` has a user-provided default constructor `B() {}`, value-initialization skips zero-initialization and directly runs `B()`, leaving `b.x` indeterminate.

questions.prompt: Why does `struct S { S() = default; int x; };` fail `S s{42};` starting in C++20 even though it compiled in C++17?
options: C++20 banned `= default` on constructors inside structs.
C++20 changed aggregate rules from 'no user-provided constructors' to 'no user-declared constructors', disqualifying S.
C++20 treats `42` as narrowing when initializing `int` in an aggregate.
questions.explanation: In C++17, `S() = default;` inside the class body was user-declared but not user-provided, so `S` remained an aggregate. C++20 ([dcl.init.aggr]) changed the requirement to 'no user-declared or inherited constructors', so `S` is no longer an aggregate and has no constructor taking `int`.

questions.prompt: Which braced conversion is NOT considered a narrowing conversion under [dcl.init.list]?
questions.explanation: Under [dcl.init.list], converting an integer type to another integer type is NOT narrowing if the source is a constant expression whose value can be represented exactly in the target type (`constexpr int ok = 100` fits in `char`). Non-constant `runtime_val`, floating-to-integer `int{d}`, and out-of-range `float{1e300}` are all ill-formed narrowing conversions.
